craft_evidence.owned: EVIDENCE: two owned woolen mills, Pendleton OR (built 1895; 'weaves all jacquard blankets and fabric for apparel') and Washougal WA (acquired 1912; 'weaves blankets and fabrics for apparel, home, upholstery'), per company fact sheet (modified 2026-06-22) and timeline; mills page documents scouring,
craft_evidence.makers: NONE: no garment maker or sewing factory named on any of 45 men's PDPs read; only assembly country.
craft_evidence.mills: Own mills only: Washougal WA named on 2 PDPs (Mill Merino, Sir Pendleton: 'Woven in our Washougal, Washington, mill'); 'woven in our American mills' on wool shirts and wool coats. No third-party cloth/yarn mill named on any PDP read.
craft_evidence.heritage: Dated and placed (claim on brand pages, consistent across fact sheet and timeline): Thomas Kay, English weaver, makes woolens in Oregon 1863; Pendleton OR mill rebuilt/opened 1909; Washougal mill acqu
craft_evidence.process: Yes for fabric: American Mills page describes scouring, dyeing (fibre/yarn/fabric), carding, spinning, weaving ('300 yards of 80-inch shirt fabric in one day'), fulling, napping, shearing, hand inspec
craft_evidence.reasoning: Pendleton owns and runs two dated woolen mills (Pendleton OR, Washougal WA) and its PDPs tie the wool shirts and wool coats to them ('Fabric woven in our American mills'; 'Assembled in El Salvador of USA made fabric'). But garments are assembled offshore and roughly 85% of the men's range (cotton shirts, tees, knitwear, canvas, chinos) is imported with no mill or maker named, so the owned making covers the cloth of a minority of styles: a 4, not a 5.

ownership.owner: Privately held, family-owned (Bishop family; 'sixth-generation family-owned business' per fact sheet); no filings

opview: “Pendleton remains a company that values craftsmanship inherited from the past, creating styles relevant for the present….” — John Bishop, Pendleton help center
